svg.title: Radio license and VHF radio equipment: what PHAK says
svg.desc: No license is required for a pilot flying in the United States; a restricted radiotelephone permit from the FCC is needed for international operation. Most general aviation radios are VHF, operating from 118.0 to 136.975 MHz, classified 720 (up to 135.975 MHz) or 760 (up to 136.975 MHz), with 25 kHz spacing. VHF is line of sight, so higher aircraft reach farther. An 8.33 kHz channel plan has been used in western Europe and the United Kingdom since January 1, 1999.
svg.text: Radio license and VHF radio equipment: what PHAK says
Operating in and out of a towered airport, and in much of the airspace system, requires two-way radio
capability.
Radio license
No license requirement for a pilot operating in
the United States
A pilot who operates internationally must hold a
restricted radiotelephone permit issued by the
FCC
No station license requirement for most general
aviation aircraft operating in the United States
A station license is required for an aircraft
that operates internationally, uses other than a
VHF radio, and meets other criteria
VHF radio
The most common type of radio in general aviation
Operates between 118.0 MHz and 136.975 MHz
Classified 720 or 760 depending on the number of
channels it can accommodate
Limited to line of sight, so aircraft at higher
altitudes can transmit and receive at greater
distances
720 and 760 radios: .025 MHz (25 kHz) spacing, for example 118.025, 118.050
The 760 reaches up to 136.975 MHz.
In March 1997 ICAO amended its standards to include a channel plan with 8.33 kHz channel spacings in the
Aeronautical Mobile Service
The plan was adopted to ease the shortage of VHF ATC channels in western Europe and the United Kingdom
Seven western European countries and the United Kingdom implemented it on January 1, 1999; aircraft
operating in the airspace of these countries must be able to transmit and receive on the 8.33 kHz spaced
channels
